strengths: Addresses a genuine and important bottleneck: amortized causal discovery methods (AVICI-style) are memory-bound at large n, and the paper demonstrates concrete gains — training at 500 nodes (where AVICI fails) and inference on 1000-node graphs with large speedups (4x–13,000x) and low inference time (0.83s at n=1000).

The architecture is well motivated and clearly described: the reduction unit (pooled compression along the observation dimension), tied attention weights for reduced attention-map memory, and the two-stream data-graph design with a data2graph message are coherently integrated, and the efficiency analysis in Section 4.6 quantifies the compute/memory savings.

Comprehensive experimental design: multiple metrics (mAP, SHD, AUC, OA, time, peak GPU memory), multiple baselines spanning constraint-based, score-based, FCM-based, and amortized paradigms, OOD mechanism tests (sigmoid, polynomial), semi-synthetic SERGIO-GRN evaluation, plus thorough ablations (reduction unit, graph stream/prior, tied vs. vanilla attention, prediction head, pooling strategy, sample size, and OOD generalization).

Solid OOD behavior on the hardest synthetic mechanism settings at n=100 (e.g., 84.4% mAP on sigmoid vs. 72.7% for SEA) and by far the best results on SERGIO-GRN, suggesting the two-stream design genuinely preserves relational information under compression rather than merely trading accuracy for speed.

Reproducibility support is reasonably good: implementation details, baseline configurations, data generation procedures, hardware, and training schedules are documented in the appendix; the impact statement appropriately cautions about treating predicted graphs as hypotheses.
weaknesses: Limited architectural novelty: the main components are adapted from prior work — tied attention from MSA Transformer (Rao et al., 2021), the decomposed prediction head from Lippe et al. (2021), and a data2graph message that is essentially average-pooling plus an outer product. The claim of being 'one of the first studies on pre-training neural networks for efficient causal discovery at scale' overstates the novelty relative to AVICI and SEA.

Potential evaluation fairness concern: AVICI is evaluated using pre-trained public checkpoints (scm-v0 / neurips-grn) rather than being retrained on the same training distribution as SEA and CauScale, which may disadvantage AVICI on their benchmarks; the paper should verify robustness of the AVICI comparison under matched training data or a stronger checkpoint.

No real-world (non-simulated) data experiments despite motivating applications in bioinformatics and citing Sachs et al. (2005); SERGIO is semi-synthetic, so claims of practical utility for scientific domains are not directly validated.

The information-preservation argument for the reduction unit is heuristic ('aggregating across samples is generally less destructive'); no theory or direct measurement of how much relational information is lost, and no analysis of when compression could harm accuracy (e.g., small-sample regimes, heavy-tailed noise).

OOD generalization remains weak in the hardest settings — e.g., polynomial mechanism at n=1000 yields only 18.9 mAP (worse than some baselines), and Figure 6 shows high sensitivity to OOD noise and functions — so the '84.4% OOD' headline figure from the abstract is not representative across the full OOD suite.

Statistical rigor is thin: results are averaged over only 5 graph instances with no confidence intervals or significance tests; the radar chart in Figure 6 reports no numbers; hyperparameter search was limited (layers in {8,10}, dims in {64,128,256}) with no discussion of sensitivity.

No acyclicity enforcement in the output; the empirical claim of low cyclicity (0.0% vs. 0.0–0.25%) is based on a small-scale ablation and would benefit from cycle statistics on the large-scale benchmark tables.

Presentation needs polish: multiple typos and grammatical issues ('It stand out', 'Tesing data', 'DaraGraph Block', 'reduction unitand'), the project page link is empty, and some notation/figure labels (e.g., Figure 1b) are hard to follow.

strengths: Targets a genuine and timely problem: amortized causal discovery methods (e.g., AVICI) scale poorly in memory with graph size, and the paper demonstrates inference on 1000-node graphs where AVICI fails, which is a useful practical result.

The evaluation is broad: multiple paradigms of baselines (constraint-based, score-based, FCM-based, amortized), four accuracy metrics plus time and peak GPU memory, ablations of each major component (reduction unit, graph stream, graph prior, tied attention, prediction head, pooling strategy), plus OOD and sample-size analyses.
The efficiency analysis in Section 4.6 is concrete and the reported compute reductions (26.64% sample-axis, 38.75% node-axis for B=10, k=2, r=2) are consistent with the design.
Appendix provides substantial implementation detail (data generation, baseline configurations, hardware, training schedule), which supports partial reproducibility of the experimental setup.
The paper is honest in parts, e.g., the generalization analysis openly reports sensitivity to OOD noise and mechanism functions.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core ingredients are all borrowed—axial attention with tied weights from Rao et al. (2021), the decomposed pairwise prediction head from Lippe et al. (2021), an inverse-covariance prior as an input feature, and standard average pooling for the reduction unit. The contribution is essentially an architectural assembly of existing components, yet the paper claims to present 'one of the first studies on pre-training neural networks for efficient causal discovery at scale,' which overclaims relative to AVICI and SEA.

Baseline fairness is questionable. AVICI is evaluated only via official pre-trained checkpoints (scm-v0, neurips-grn) while SEA and CauScale are trained on the authors' own training data (Appendix C). This makes the headline AVICI comparisons (e.g., 4x speedup, mAP gaps, OOM claims) confounded: a poorly matched checkpoint plausibly explains both AVICI's low mAP (0.2 on n=1000 linear) and the OOM results. The AVICI OOM even at n=100 on an H200 with 141GB also seems surprising and needs explanation (context limits? batching choices?).

Near-perfect in-distribution results (99.6% mAP, SHD 15.2 on linear data) suggest the benchmark may be nearly solvable with the covariance-based prior alone (INVCOV already reaches 99.8 AUC), weakening the evidential value of the headline numbers; the truly discriminative settings show much weaker performance (polynomial OOD: 18.9 mAP at n=1000, worse than CORR's 25.0), which contradicts the abstract's framing of strong OOD robustness.

The reduction unit's justification is heuristic. Claim (2) that aggregating across i.i.d. samples is 'generally less destructive' is asserted without theory or an information-theoretic argument, and discarding the last m−m̂ samples is ad hoc. The Design/Reduced-information-loss motivations are plausibility arguments, not evidence.

Only 5 independent graph instances per configuration are used, with no variance or significance reporting; several conclusions (e.g., OOD generalization patterns in Figure 6, the pooling comparison in Table 2) could be noise at this sample size.

Writing and presentation issues undermine confidence: multiple typos ('It stand out', 'Tesing data', 'reduction unitand', 'DaraGraph Block' in Figure 2, 'axis' for 'axes'), an empty project page URL ('Our project page is at .'), and inconsistent notation (m vs. m̂, N vs. n for graph size). No code release is confirmed despite claims of reproducibility.

Only simulated data (synthetic SCMs and SERGIO semi-synthetic GRNs) are used; there is no real-world benchmark (e.g., Sachs protein data), so claims of practical utility in bioinformatics remain unverified.

The claim that the decomposed head 'empirically produces fewer cycles' is supported only by Figure 5 on small graphs (n≤100), and the training-cost asymmetry is not discussed: CauScale's training requires 37+2.75 GPU-hours on 8 H200s plus a two-stage schedule, while the paper's efficiency narrative focuses solely on inference time.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated bottleneck: amortized causal discovery methods (AVICI, SEA) scale poorly in time/memory with graph size, and CauScale's combination of a reduction unit (progressive pooling along the sample axis), tied attention weights, and a two-stream data/graph design is a sensible and clearly described engineering solution.

Comprehensive experimental coverage: multiple paradigms of baselines (constraint-based, score-based, FCM-based, amortized), four accuracy metrics plus inference time and peak GPU memory, ablations of every major component (reduction unit, graph prior, graph stream, tied attention, prediction head, pooling strategy), and OOD generalization analysis across graph structures, noise, and mechanisms.

The scaling results are compelling: training on 500-node graphs where AVICI OOMs, and inference on 1000-node graphs with sub-second runtime, are concrete demonstrations that the efficiency goals were met.

The motivation for the reduction unit (compress along the observation dimension under i.i.d. sampling rather than the variable dimension, and distill relational evidence into the graph stream before compression) is well argued and supported by the ablation in Figure 3.
Reproducibility is aided by a detailed appendix: data generation procedures, baseline implementations with thresholds, hardware, training schedules, and hyperparameter search space.
weaknesses: Baseline fairness is a significant concern. AVICI is evaluated with pre-trained checkpoints (scm-v0, neurips-grn) rather than being trained on the same data distribution as CauScale and SEA, while CauScale is trained in-distribution on the exact simulator and graph families used at test time. This makes the headline accuracy comparisons (e.g., AVICI mAP 25.9 vs. CauScale 99.6 at n=100; AVICI 0.2 at n=1000) difficult to interpret—the central claim of 'superior accuracy' partly rests on an uneven comparison. At minimum, the paper needs an AVICI variant fine-tuned/trained on the same distributions, or a clear caveat separating these comparisons.

The near-perfect in-distribution results (99.6% mAP, SHD 15.2, 100% OA on linear data) raise questions about how much is learned relational structure vs. simulator-specific cues. Test graphs are Erdős–Rényi instances from the same generation pipeline as training, and the inverse-covariance prior alone achieves high AUC. Only 5 graph instances per configuration are averaged, with no variance or significance reporting.

The method assumes single-node interventional data covering all nodes (1:n observational:interventional ratio for synthetic; gene knockouts for GRN data). This is a strong practical assumption that limits applicability to many real settings, and it is not adequately discussed as a limitation or ablated (e.g., performance with purely observational data).

Originality is modest: tied attention is borrowed from MSA Transformer (Rao et al., 2021), the reduction unit is average pooling along the sample axis, and the two-stream/data2graph design is an incremental combination of known components. The claim of being 'one of the first studies on pre-training neural networks for efficient causal discovery at scale' overstates novelty given AVICI and SEA.

Speedup claims of 4x–13,000x are partly apples-to-oranges: the largest speedups come against non-amortized methods (NOTEARS) that solve a per-dataset optimization, which is the well-known motivation for amortization rather than a novel contribution of this paper.

Reproducibility gaps: no code release is evidenced (the project page link in the abstract is empty), and results lack error bars. Reproducing a two-stage, 8-GPU training pipeline without code would be difficult.

Presentation quality is below bar in places: typos and grammatical errors ('It stand out', 'Tesing data', 'DaraGraph Block', 'w/o reduction unitand', 'axis' for 'axes'), a truncated project-page URL, and some over-claimed phrasing. The limitations discussion is implicit (OOD sensitivity in Fig. 6) rather than an explicit treatment.

Sample-size analysis (Fig. 7) shows performance degrading at inference sample sizes above the training sample size (peak at 2000 for synthetic data trained with 1000), suggesting the model is sensitive to distribution shift in m, but this is observed rather than analyzed or mitigated.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practically important bottleneck—time and memory scalability of amortized causal discovery—and the proposed combination (reduction unit pooling along the observation axis, tied axial attention weights, two-stream data-graph design with a distillation-style data-graph block) is coherent and well-motivated, with three explicit justifications for why compressing the observation axis is preferable to subsampling or variable-axis compression.

The experimental evaluation is unusually comprehensive for this area: multiple metrics (SHD, mAP, AUC, OA, AID family, cyclicity), multiple baselines spanning four methodological paradigms, ablations of every major component (reduction unit, graph prior, graph stream, tied attention, prediction head, pooling strategy), and robustness studies on latent confounders, prior-sample sensitivity, sample-size sensitivity, and multiple OOD axes (graph structure, mechanism, noise).

The efficiency analysis is substantive rather than superficial: FLOP-level accounting of each sublayer (Appendix E), a memory proposition with proof, and empirical time/memory measurements supporting the claimed 4x-13,000x speedups and the ability to run inference on 1000-node graphs where AVICI goes out of memory.

The identification of cyclicity in OOD predictions, quantification of it (Table 2), and a simple confidence-guided cycle-breaking procedure is a useful practical contribution, and the paper honestly notes SDCD's 100% cyclic outputs would otherwise invalidate AID comparisons.
The limitations are discussed candidly (dependence on simulated training data, deviation from SCM assumptions), and there is a supporting impact statement.
weaknesses: Baseline fairness concerns weaken the headline accuracy claims. AVICI is evaluated only via pretrained public checkpoints (scm-v0, neuroips-grn) rather than retrained on the same data as CauScale and SEA, whereas SEA is explicitly retrained on the authors' training data. AVICI's very low mAP (e.g., 25.9/33.3 at n=100) may substantially understate what a properly trained AVICI could achieve on this distribution, so the claim of superior discovery quality over prior amortized methods is not fully supported.

The headline numbers are somewhat cherry-picked: 99.6% mAP refers to the easiest setting (linear, in-distribution, with 1:n interventional samples), while the hardest OOD setting (polynomial, n=1000) drops to 18.9% mAP with ~3985 SHD, worse than several baselines (Table 5 shows CauScale is not best on polynomial AID at n=1000 either). Table 4 further shows that with only 500 prior samples at n=1000, mAP is 64.9%, indicating meaningful sensitivity to prior quality precisely in the large-graph regime the paper emphasizes.

Originality is moderate: the individual ingredients (axial attention, tied attention weights from Rao et al. 2021, average-pooling-based reduction, the decomposed prediction head from Wu et al. 2025) are existing techniques, and the claim of being 'one of the first studies on pre-training neural networks for causal discovery at scale' overstates novelty given AVICI already established amortized/pretrained causal discovery. The contribution is primarily an efficiency-oriented architectural engineering effort.

The reliance on a statistical graph prior (inverse covariance matrix) raises questions about how much of the near-perfect linear performance derives from a linear-Gaussian sufficient statistic rather than learned causal inference; while the ablation shows the prior matters less than the graph stream, the prior's behavior under non-Gaussian or heavily nonlinear OOD mechanisms deserves more analysis.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the project page link in the abstract appears blank, no code release is explicitly promised, training requires substantial resources (8 GPUs, ~37 hours stage 1), and several key details (e.g., number of samples used for the prior in the main Table 1, the two-stage training curriculum's interaction with results) must be pieced together from the appendix.

Testing is limited to 5 graphs per configuration, and evaluation on real-world observational datasets is absent (acknowledged), which constrains the external validity of claims about 'causal discovery at scale.'

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely relevant problem: existing amortized causal discovery methods (AVICI, etc.) scale poorly in time and memory, and the demonstrated ability to train on 500-node graphs and perform zero-shot inference on 1000-node graphs is a concrete, useful capability that prior amortized baselines cannot match (AVICI OOMs even at n=100 with 20k samples on SERGIO-GRN).

The experimental section is broad: multiple baselines spanning four paradigms, eight structure-learning metrics plus runtime and GPU memory, ablations of every major component (reduction unit, tied attention, graph stream, graph prior, prediction head, pooling strategy), and additional analyses of OOD generalization, latent confounders, prior-sample sensitivity, and sample-size effects.

The efficiency analysis is more careful than typical: the paper provides a FLOP-level accounting of the forward pass (Appendix E) and a formal Proposition E.1 with proof for peak inference activation memory, complementing the empirical time/memory measurements.

The limitations are discussed honestly, including reliance on simulated training data, lack of real-world evaluation, and sensitivity to OOD noise/mechanisms; the impact statement appropriately cautions against use in high-stakes settings without expert validation.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The three core ingredients are largely borrowed: tied attention weights are taken directly from Rao et al. (2021) (MSA Transformer), the decomposed three-state prediction head is adopted from Wu et al. (2025)/Lippe et al. (2021), and the 'reduction unit' is average pooling along the sample axis every k blocks. The overall contribution is an engineering combination of known techniques applied to amortized causal discovery rather than a new method or new understanding; the claim of 'one of the first studies on pre-training neural networks for efficient causal discovery' overstates the contribution given AVICI (2022) and SEA (2025) already occupy this space.

Evaluation is essentially confined to synthetic and semi-synthetic data. There is no real-world observational dataset (e.g., Sachs protein signaling, which the paper itself cites), so the claimed practical utility for 'scientific AI and data analysis' is not substantiated. The authors acknowledge this, but for a paper whose central pitch is scalability and practical efficiency, this is a material gap.

Baseline fairness is inconsistent. AVICI is evaluated using off-the-shelf pre-trained checkpoints (scm-v0, neurips-grn) rather than being trained on the same data distribution as CauScale, making the very large accuracy gaps on in-distribution synthetic data (e.g., 99.6 vs 25.9 mAP on linear n=100) difficult to interpret. SEA is retrained on matched data, but only for some settings. This weakens the headline claim of 'superior accuracy' over prior methods.

OOD robustness is weaker than the abstract suggests. The advertised 84.4% OOD mAP appears to reflect the favorable sigmoid setting; on the polynomial OOD mechanism at n=1000 CauScale achieves only 18.9 ± 13.8 mAP (SHD 3985 ± 2975, cycle fraction 1.0 requiring removal of ~103 edges per graph). With only 5 test graphs, several headline numbers have very large variance, and the abstract does not convey this fragility.

The graph prior rho = inverse covariance matrix is problematic and under-specified: at the flagship test setting n=1000 with only m=1000 samples, the sample covariance is singular, yet the paper does not explain how the inverse is computed or regularized (Hartlap et al. is cited but no shrinkage procedure is described). Additionally, for CORR/INVCOV baselines the discretization threshold is set using the ground-truth edge count, which leaks oracle information into these reference points.

Several empirical claims are not fully supported or are internally ambiguous. The reduction-unit ablation is run on a reduced training subset (n <= 100) rather than the full training distribution, so its effect at the scale where the paper claims its main advantage (n up to 500/1000) is extrapolated; Figure 3 appears to show the w/o-reduction variant attaining slightly higher mAP at the largest tested size, which sits uneasily with the claim of 'maintaining high accuracy'.

Presentation has notable sloppiness that undermines confidence: 'DaraGraph Block' (Fig. 2 caption), 'Tesing data', 'It stand out', 'reduction unitand', an empty project-page URL, and inconsistent capitalization of method names. The paper also relies on interventional data (1:n interventional/observational ratio) for training without clearly flagging that the method's strong performance depends on this assumption, which many practical deployment settings cannot satisfy.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly positioned contribution: addressing time- and memory-bottlenecks of amortized causal discovery (AVICI, SEA) is a practical problem, and the proposed combination of a reduction unit (progressive pooling of the data/stream dimension), tied attention weights, and a two-stream data-graph design is coherent and well explained with clear figures and a detailed FLOP/memory analysis (Appendix E, Proposition E.1).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: strong baseline coverage (FCI, NOTEARS, SDCD, DiffAN, AVICI, SEA plus CORR/INVCOV reference points), eight metrics including the modern AID family, ablations of every major component (reduction unit, graph stream, graph prior, attention mechanism, prediction head, pooling strategy), and additional analyses of generalization, latent confounding, prior-sample sensitivity, and sample size.

Impressive scalability results: training up to 500 nodes, inference on 1000-node graphs (beyond the training distribution), and success where AVICI runs out of memory even at n=100 with 20,000 samples in the SERGIO-GRN setting; large reported speedups (4x–13,000x).

Transparent treatment of weaknesses: the paper honestly reports mechanism-specific OOD failures (e.g., polynomial at n=1000 drops to 18.9 mAP), cycle-breaking effects, and acknowledges in the conclusion that evaluation is limited to simulated/semi-synthetic data. Implementation details, hardware, training schedules, and baseline configurations are documented thoroughly, which supports reproducibility in principle.
weaknesses: Limited technical originality: the core ingredients are largely borrowed or simple—tied attention is taken directly from Rao et al. (2021), the prediction head from Wu et al. (2025)/Lippe et al. (2021), and the reduction unit is essentially average pooling over the sample axis. The novelty is an architectural combination rather than a new method or new understanding, and the claim of 'one of the first studies on pre-training neural networks for causal discovery' overstates novelty given AVICI and related amortized work.

Baseline comparability concerns: AVICI is evaluated only with pre-trained checkpoints (not retrained on the same training data as CaScale and SEA), so the accuracy and speed comparisons against the closest amortized competitor are not fully fair. Additionally, CORR/INVCOV baselines are thresholded using the ground-truth edge count (oracle sparsity knowledge), and it is unclear whether CaScale's discretization receives the same oracle advantage.

Information-loss justification for the reduction unit is heuristic: the three motivating arguments (efficiency, dependency structure, reduced information loss) are intuitive but no theory or direct evidence shows what information the pooling discards, and the ablation (Figure 3) partly conflates training efficiency with inference-time benefits.

Real-world validity untested: all experiments use synthetic SCMs and SERGIO simulation; no genuine observational dataset (e.g., Sachs protein data, which the paper itself cites) is evaluated. Combined with Gaussian-flavored statistical priors (inverse covariance) and training only on ER/Scale-Free graphs, external validity remains an open question the paper defers to future work.

Headline OOD claim is optimistic: the abstract's '84.4% on out-of-distribution data' averages across mechanisms and hides that performance on the hardest OOD mechanism (polynomial, n=1000) is 18.9±13.8 mAP with very high variance across only 5 test graphs; several results have large standard deviations, so some claims rest on weak statistical support.

Reproducibility gap: the abstract references a project page that appears blank/incomplete ('Our project page is .'), and no code release is explicitly stated; given the two-stage training on 8 GPUs and extensive hyperparameter details, released code would be important for others to build on this work.

Some design choices are under-analyzed: cycle-breaking at n=1000 removes ~103 edges per graph on polynomial data, indicating substantial failure mode at scale that the main narrative does not emphasize; the latent-confounder simulation (removing top out-degree hub nodes) is a somewhat artificial proxy for confounding.
